title: Reading a quantum-oncology headline
summary: Seven questions that expose most overclaims — claim, comparator, scale, data, endpoint, evidence level and source — applied to real announcements, then your own audit.

shots.title:
Reading a
headline.
shots.subtitle: Seven questions, every time.
shots.narration: Headlines about quantum computing and cancer arrive weekly. Seven questions sort most of them in a few minutes — and they are the same questions referees will ask of your paper.

shots.heading: Four questions about the claim
shots.narration: Four questions about the claim itself. Claim: exactly what, with which number. Comparator: against which classical method, tuned how. Scale: could a laptop simulate it. Data: leakage-free and externally validated?

shots.heading: Three about the evidence
items: **Source** — who says so; who replicated it?
shots.narration: And three about the evidence. Endpoint: does it matter clinically. Evidence: peer-reviewed paper, preprint or press release. Source: who says so, and has anyone independent replicated it?

shots.text: “First quantum computer **dedicated to healthcare**” — a fact about **deployment**, not about results.
shots.narration: Example one: the first quantum computer dedicated to healthcare research. True as stated — and it tells you about a deployment, not about any result.

shots.text: “Quantum computing finds cancer-drug candidates” — molecules were made and tested; **quantum necessity** was not shown.
shots.narration: Example two: quantum computing finds cancer-drug candidates. Molecules were indeed made and tested. But sixteen qubits are classically simulable, so the scale question already tells you quantum hardware was not necessary.

shots.text: “Quantum annealing classifies cancer better with little data” — a **random-bit-string control** did as well.
shots.narration: Example three: quantum annealing classifies cancers better with little data. The comparator question finds the answer in the paper itself: random bit-strings ranked by the same objective did as well.

shots.text: “Team wins quantum-for-health prize” — for a **scalable demonstration**, by design **not** for advantage.
shots.narration: Example four: a team wins a quantum-for-health prize. Read the prize rules: it rewarded a scalable demonstration on more than fifty qubits. Advantage had its own prize, and no winner for it was announced.

Example five: beyond brute-force classical simulation. That is not the same as beyond all classical methods — IBM's 2023 utility experiment was later reproduced by tensor networks more accurately than the quantum hardware.

shots.label: smaller median effect sizes when cancer-biology experiments were replicated
shots.context: 50 experiments from 23 high-impact papers · 46% replicated on most criteria
shots.narration: Keep base rates in mind. When fifty experiments from twenty-three high-impact cancer-biology papers were repeated, effect sizes were a median eighty-five percent smaller, and under half replicated on most criteria. Novel results shrink.

shots.text: Your audit: one real announcement, seven questions, a **verdict** with a confidence.
shots.narration: Now your turn: pick one real announcement, answer the seven questions with sources, and give a verdict with a confidence level. It is the same skill as writing a careful discussion section.

steps.title: Which question catches it?
steps.brief: Each card is a weakness hidden in a hypothetical announcement. Which of the seven questions exposes it?

cards.text: The quantum model beat an SVM with default settings
cards.why: An untuned baseline is a straw man.

cards.text: The comparison was against random search, not simulated annealing
cards.why: Compare with the strongest classical heuristic.

cards.text: Accuracy was measured on the patients used for feature selection
No external cohort; one hospital's data
Results appear only in a company press release
cards.why: No methods, no peer review, no data.

cards.text: A preprint called “verified” in the headline
cards.why: Preprints are not yet peer-reviewed; they can be right, but say so.

steps.title: Headline audit
steps.brief: Pick a real announcement. Answer the seven questions with sources (the course ledger, or primary sources you find).

fields.label: Which announcement are you auditing?
options: Quantum feature selection for cancer biomarkers (Infleqtion, 2026)

fields.label: Claim — exactly what, with its number.
Comparator and scale — classical baseline, tuning, qubits, simulability.
Data and endpoint — what data, how validated, does the endpoint matter clinically?
How much should an oncology research group change its plans because of this?
Your verdict, in two or three sentences.

questions.prompt: A headline says a quantum method beat classical machine learning on cancer data. Which question do you ask first?
options: Which classical method, tuned how, on which data split?
questions.explain: The comparator and the validation decide whether “beat” means anything.

options: No classical method can reproduce it
Storing the full state vector is infeasible — other classical methods may still work
questions.explain: Tensor networks and other methods can succeed where brute force fails.

steps.title: Watch: the quantum shift in biomedical discovery
steps.caption: A podcast episode published by IBM: Malcolm Gladwell talks with Lara Jehi of the Cleveland Clinic–IBM Discovery Accelerator about AI and quantum computing in biomedical research. It is promotional, so use it to practise this lesson's audit — which statements are demonstrations, and which are hopes?

steps.title: Listen: is quantum computing having its moment?
steps.caption: BBC Inside Science visits ORCA Computing in London, after the UK government announced a large quantum fund, to ask how close the quantum future is; the segment opens the episode. Notice who is speaking each time — company, government or independent scientist.
